title: FBLA governance and current-season preparation
summary: How FBLA is organized and where to find its rules and programs.

sections.heading: How FBLA is organized
paragraphs: FBLA has Middle School, High School, and Collegiate student divisions, with local and state structures. Corporate bylaws address the overall organization; division bylaws address that division. The corporate board manages the organization, while the president and CEO administers its affairs. Student officer leadership differs from staff administration. The current corporate bylaws define the membership and fiscal year as August 1 through July 31. Always compare document versions when studying governance.

sections.heading: Recognize programs and partners
paragraphs: The official high-school page highlights LifeSmarts, Virtual Business Challenge, the Stock Market Game, and Lead4Change as education programs. Learn what a program develops, not just its logo: consumer knowledge, business decision-making, investing simulation, or service leadership. A partner or sponsor supplies a relationship or opportunity; it is not automatically a rulemaking body. Use official program and partner pages for current descriptions, availability, and requirements.

Examples on the current official partner page include the National Consumers League’s LifeSmarts consumer-education program, the College Board relationship around AP Business with Personal Finance, and AICPA career resources for exploring accounting. Tomorrow’s Business Leader is identified on FBLA’s publication page as its flagship magazine, featuring organization updates, chapter achievements, alumni, and business perspectives. Archived issues can teach context but do not set current event deadlines.

sections.heading: Check the season and competition stage
paragraphs: Use current event guidelines for the event and stage, the operations manual for shared procedures, and the Honor Code, Code of Conduct, and Dress Code for participation expectations. Official communications and CONNECT provide current updates and member resources. Maryland district instructions can differ from later stages. Record the season, jurisdiction, document date, and deadline purpose. A chapter’s internal deadline may be earlier. No fixed weighting is published for Future Business Leader’s broad test, so these readings do not claim a complete test blueprint.

The Dress Code supports a professional appearance at conferences; examine the actual illustrated official policy for permitted attire rather than relying on an old summary. Read the Honor Code for independent work and conduct expectations. A current competition sheet should record event name, season, stage, format, materials, timing, scoring, and submission obligations. Current Maryland dates belong in the Maryland Guide so a change does not leave conflicting dates scattered through lessons.

example.scenario: A national role-play event is test-only at Maryland districts.
example.solution: Prepare for the district test now and retain the later-stage role-play requirements separately. Do not import the national format into the district checklist.

The authority or competition level to which a rule applies.

title: Parliamentary foundations and meeting structure
summary: Meeting rules, members’ rights, and the roles of officers.

sections.heading: Know the authority and basic terms
paragraphs: Parliamentary procedure helps an assembly decide business fairly and efficiently, balancing majority decision with minority participation and individual rights. A quorum is the minimum required attendance to transact business. The chair presides, a member has the floor when recognized to speak, and a pending motion awaits disposal. Applicable law and governing documents take priority over default parliamentary rules. Maryland’s guide identifies Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised, 12th edition, for this event.

A useful hierarchy places applicable law and the corporate charter above bylaws, followed by special rules of order and the adopted parliamentary authority; standing rules address administration. Check the organization’s actual documents. One question at a time means the assembly resolves the immediately pending question before returning to the underlying business; it does not mean subsidiary motions can never interrupt a main motion.

sections.heading: Use an orderly meeting
paragraphs: A standard order includes reading and approval of minutes, officer and board reports, committee reports, special orders, unfinished business and general orders, then new business. Minutes record what was done rather than a transcript of everything said. Correct minutes through the approval process. The chair maintains impartiality, states questions clearly, manages debate, and announces results. The secretary preserves the record. A special meeting is limited by its call and governing rules.

example.scenario: Several members leave and attendance falls below the quorum.
example.solution: Do not continue substantive decisions as if the original attendance permanently established a quorum. Follow permitted procedural steps and restore attendance before transacting business.

sections.heading: Distinguish roles and documents
paragraphs: A president leads while presiding impartially; a vice president performs assigned duties and substitutes as appropriate; the treasurer reports finances; the secretary maintains records. “Pro tem” means serving temporarily, while “ex officio” means membership by virtue of another office. Voting rights depend on applicable rules; an organization can expressly create a nonvoting position. Executive session is confidential, not a license to disregard rules. Study the actual bylaws before assuming every organization follows an identical procedure.

Previous notice alerts members that specified business will be proposed under applicable timing and content rules. The notice can affect the vote required for actions such as rescinding. A notice requirement is not satisfied merely because someone privately mentioned an idea.

terms.definition: The minimum attendance required for conducting substantive business.
Serving temporarily in a role.

questions.prompt: A quorum is:
questions.explanation: It concerns attendance, not votes for a motion.

questions.prompt: Minutes primarily record:
questions.explanation: Minutes preserve actions rather than a full transcript of debate.

questions.prompt: Which takes priority over default parliamentary rules?
questions.explanation: RONR supplies default rules subject to higher authority.

questions.prompt: Ex officio means:
choices: Without a vote in every case
questions.explanation: The term describes why a person holds membership, not automatically whether they vote.

questions.prompt: After quorum is lost, the assembly may:
choices: Declare every earlier action void automatically
Not transact substantive business without quorum
questions.explanation: Quorum must be present for substantive business.

title: Motions, amendments, and debate
summary: How to introduce a motion, amend it, and handle debate.

sections.heading: Follow the six-step main-motion path
paragraphs: A member obtains recognition and makes a motion; another member seconds it when required; the chair states the question; members debate; the chair puts the question to a vote; the chair announces the result. A second means another member wants consideration, not necessarily agreement. Once stated by the chair, the motion belongs to the assembly. Amendments change wording and must be germane; vote on an amendment before the affected main motion.

example.scenario: A member moves to spend $100; an amendment changes $100 to $80.
example.solution: Resolve the amendment first. If adopted, then debate and vote on the main motion to spend $80. Adopting the amendment alone does not adopt the spending proposal.

sections.heading: Choose the right class
paragraphs: Main motions introduce business. Subsidiary motions help dispose of a pending question, such as amend, commit, or postpone. Privileged motions address urgent assembly needs. Incidental motions handle procedural questions arising from business, such as a point of order or appeal. Motions bringing a question again before the assembly include reconsider and rescind. Laying on the table temporarily sets aside business for an urgent matter; it should not be confused with postponing to a chosen time or defeating a proposal.

sections.heading: Manage precedence and debate
paragraphs: Higher-ranking motions can take precedence over lower-ranking pending motions in the relevant circumstances. Study both rank and the rule for debate, amendment, and voting; not every motion is debatable or requires the same threshold. Address remarks to the chair and discuss the question without personal attacks. A demand for an immediate vote is not automatically adopted: the previous question requires the appropriate vote. Consult the adopted authority for exceptions, qualifications, and special circumstances.

In an ordinary deliberative assembly under default rules, a member ordinarily has up to two speeches on the same question in one day, up to ten minutes each, and must yield priority to someone who has not spoken. The assembly’s rules can change these limits. A primary amendment can itself be amended once; an amendment to an amendment is resolved before the primary amendment. Reconsider generally concerns a recent vote and has special maker and timing requirements. Rescind addresses an earlier action, subject to notice, vote, and limits on what can be undone.

rows: Dispose without a direct vote on the main question
Change debate limits; normally two thirds
Temporarily set aside for urgent intervening business
Call for orders of the day
Require the adopted order, subject to applicable rules
Fix the time to which to adjourn

terms.definition: Before the assembly and not yet disposed of.
Relevant to the subject of the motion being amended.

questions.prompt: A second normally means:
questions.explanation: A seconder may later oppose the motion.

questions.prompt: An amendment passes. What follows?
choices: Consider the main motion as amended
questions.explanation: The amendment changes the pending main motion; it does not itself adopt that motion.

questions.prompt: A point of order is generally:
questions.explanation: It raises a procedural rule issue arising from business.

questions.prompt: Which changes a motion’s wording?
questions.explanation: An amendment proposes a germane change.

choices: No; the required procedure and vote apply
questions.explanation: Closing debate requires proper handling of the previous question, usually a two-thirds vote.

title: Voting, elections, boards, and committees
summary: Voting thresholds, election methods, and the authority of boards and committees.

sections.heading: Count the correct denominator
paragraphs: A majority is more than half; a two-thirds requirement is at least two thirds, without rounding down. A plurality is the largest number and need not be a majority. Under ordinary votes-cast rules, abstentions are not votes; rules based on members present or total membership behave differently. Check the stated denominator before calculating. Tie votes fail when a majority is required.

example.scenario: Seventeen votes are cast. How many affirmative votes are needed?
example.solution: A majority needs nine. Two thirds of 17 is 11.33, so a two-thirds requirement needs twelve. Do not round down.

sections.heading: Choose a method and conduct elections
paragraphs: Voice votes suit ordinary questions; rising or counted votes clarify results; ballots can protect secrecy and may be required by rules. A division requests a rising vote under the applicable procedure; it is not automatically a demand for a roll call. Nominations propose candidates, while election votes select them. A presiding member’s voting rights depend on the body, method, and rules; “the chair only votes to break ties” is an inaccurate universal rule. Do not assume plurality elects when a majority is required.

Unanimous consent allows routine action when the chair asks for objection and no one objects. An objection does not itself defeat the proposal; it requires handling it through the regular procedure. In a large assembly, the chair ordinarily remains impartial and votes by ballot or when the vote affects the result under the applicable rules. Small boards and committees can follow different procedures.

sections.heading: Use committees and boards within authority
paragraphs: Standing committees handle continuing work; special committees serve a defined task. Referral sends a pending matter for study and recommendation as authorized. A committee report can recommend action, but the assembly may still need to adopt the recommendation. Boards operate under powers granted by the governing documents; they are not automatically above the membership in every matter. Record scope, deadline, resources, and reporting responsibility so delegation does not become unexplained authority.

terms.definition: More than half of the applicable voting base.
A committee for continuing responsibilities.

questions.prompt: A majority of 17 votes cast is at least:
questions.explanation: Nine is more than half of seventeen.

questions.prompt: A two-thirds vote out of 17 needs at least:
questions.explanation: The threshold is at least 11.33, so twelve affirmative votes are required.

questions.prompt: Under ordinary votes-cast rules, abstentions:
questions.explanation: Abstention means not voting; special denominator rules can change the practical effect.

questions.prompt: A committee for an ongoing budget function is usually:
questions.explanation: Standing committees handle recurring responsibilities.

questions.prompt: A committee recommendation automatically becomes assembly policy:
choices: No; assembly action may still be needed
questions.explanation: The authority and required adoption procedure depend on the governing rules.

title: Business technology and customer value
summary: Marketing basics, business information systems, and data security.

sections.heading: Start with the customer
paragraphs: Marketing identifies, creates, communicates, and delivers value; it is broader than advertising. Segment a market into meaningful groups, select a target, and position the offering against relevant alternatives. Product, price, place, and promotion must work together. A lower price will not fix an inaccessible distribution channel. Research can use primary data collected for the question or secondary data already available; check sampling, bias, and source quality.

Positioning is the intended place in the customer’s mind, not merely physical shelf space. Research quality depends on asking a clear question, choosing a relevant sample, avoiding leading wording, and using a meaningful comparison. A campaign measure should connect to its goal: reach concerns exposure, engagement concerns response, conversion concerns a desired action, and retention concerns continued relationships.

sections.heading: Use information systems purposefully
paragraphs: Hardware, software, networks, data, people, and procedures work together in a business information system. A database stores related records, while a spreadsheet supports flexible calculation and analysis. Data quality requires accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness. A dashboard summarizes selected measures, not all reality. Algorithms follow instructions; a plausible automated output still needs validation. Distinguish a correlation from proof of cause when interpreting business data.

example.scenario: Website visits rise from 1,000 to 2,000, but orders remain 50.
example.solution: The conversion rate falls from 5% to 2.5%. More traffic alone does not show better sales performance. Investigate traffic quality and the purchase process.

sections.heading: Protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability
paragraphs: Confidentiality limits unauthorized disclosure, integrity protects accuracy and authorized change, and availability supports access when needed. Use unique strong authentication, timely updates, least-privilege access, and tested backups. Phishing manipulates people into unsafe actions; verify unusual requests independently. A backup is useful only if restoration works. Responsible technology use includes privacy, accessibility, citation, licensing, and review of automated content. Future Business Leader has a broad general-business and technology area rather than a closed list of every possible question.

terms.definition: Desired actions divided by the relevant opportunities, such as orders per visit.
Giving only the access needed for a role.

questions.prompt: Marketing is:
choices: The broader work of creating and delivering customer value
questions.explanation: Advertising is one promotional activity within marketing.

questions.prompt: 50 orders from 2,000 visits gives conversion of:
Protecting data against unauthorized changes supports:
questions.explanation: Integrity concerns accuracy and authorized changes.

questions.prompt: A tested backup mainly supports:
questions.explanation: Restoration testing shows whether data can actually be recovered.

questions.prompt: A suspicious urgent credential request should be:
choices: Verified independently through a known channel
questions.explanation: Independent verification reduces phishing risk.

title: Accounting cycle workbook: one month of books
summary: Follow a fictional business from source documents to the post-closing trial balance, then find and correct common errors.

sections.heading: The ten steps in order
paragraphs: Objective tests often ask which step comes next or which step a document belongs to. Learn the order as a chain where each step uses the output of the one before it. Source documents prove that a transaction happened. The journal records each transaction in date order. The ledger groups those entries by account. The trial balance tests whether total debits equal total credits.

Adjusting entries come after the unadjusted trial balance and before the statements. They are made at the end of the period and never involve cash. Closing entries come after the statements because the statements need the revenue and expense balances before they are reset to zero.
steps: Collect and analyze source documents such as invoices, receipts, checks, and deposit slips.
Journalize each transaction in the general journal or a special journal.
Post journal amounts to ledger accounts.
Prepare the unadjusted trial balance.
Record and post adjusting entries.
Prepare the adjusted trial balance, often on a worksheet.
Prepare the income statement, statement of owner's equity, and balance sheet.
Journalize and post closing entries.
Prepare the post-closing trial balance.
Optionally record reversing entries on the first day of the next period.

sections.heading: Record a month of transactions
paragraphs: Lantern Lawn Care is a fictional sole proprietorship that starts business on June 1. The table shows each transaction, the entry, and the reason. Read the reason column carefully. The most common test errors come from treating owner investment as revenue, treating a customer advance as revenue, or treating a prepayment as an expense.

rows: Owner investment raises equity but is not revenue.
2. Buys equipment for $2,400: $600 cash, rest on account
One entry can have several credits if the totals match.
The coverage has not been used yet, so it is an asset.
Supplies are an asset until used.
Revenue is earned when the work is done.
7. Receives $400 in advance for July work
The business owes the work, so this is a liability.
One asset rises and another falls. No revenue.
Paying a debt is not an expense.
Withdrawals reduce equity but are not expenses.

example.scenario: After posting, what is the Cash balance, and does the unadjusted trial balance balance?
steps: Accounts Receivable: 900 - 500 = 400. Accounts Payable: 1,800 + 300 - 1,000 = 1,100.
Debit balances: Cash 3,600 + A/R 400 + Supplies 300 + Prepaid Insurance 1,200 + Equipment 2,400 + Drawing 300 + Wages Expense 700 = 8,900.
Credit balances: A/P 1,100 + Unearned Revenue 400 + Capital 5,000 + Service Revenue 2,400 = 8,900.
example.solution: Cash is $3,600 and both columns total $8,900, so the unadjusted trial balance is in balance. A balanced trial balance still does not prove every entry is correct.

sections.heading: Adjust at the end of the month
paragraphs: Each adjustment fixes the timing of a revenue or expense so the month shows what was actually earned and used. Every adjusting entry affects one income statement account and one balance sheet account. Cash is never part of an adjusting entry.

Lantern counts $120 of supplies left on June 30, so $180 was used. One month of the 12-month policy has expired, which is $1,200 / 12 = $100. Equipment costing $2,400 with a 4-year life and no salvage value depreciates $600 a year, or $50 a month. Lantern completed $150 of the work customers paid for in advance. Employees earned $200 of wages that will be paid in July. Lantern also finished $250 of work that has not been billed yet.
bullets: Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset with a credit balance. Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation: 2,400 - 50 = 2,350.
After adjustment, Service Revenue is 2,400 + 150 + 250 = 2,800 and Wages Expense is 700 + 200 = 900.
The adjusted trial balance totals $9,400 on each side.

sections.heading: Prepare the three statements
paragraphs: Prepare the statements in this order because each one feeds the next. Net income from the income statement goes to the statement of owner's equity. Ending capital from that statement goes to the balance sheet.
Income statement: Service Revenue 2,800. Expenses are Wages 900, Supplies 180, Insurance 100, and Depreciation 50, for a total of 1,230. Net income is 1,570.
Statement of owner's equity: Beginning capital 0, plus investment 5,000, plus net income 1,570, minus drawing 300, equals ending capital 6,270.

Balance sheet: Cash 3,600, Accounts Receivable 650, Supplies 120, Prepaid Insurance 1,100, and Equipment at book value 2,350 give total assets of 7,820. Liabilities are Accounts Payable 1,100, Wages Payable 200, and Unearned Revenue 250, for 1,550. Liabilities 1,550 plus equity 6,270 equal 7,820, so the equation balances.

sections.heading: Close the books
paragraphs: Closing moves the period's revenue, expense, and drawing balances into capital so those temporary accounts start July at zero. Permanent accounts, which are the balance sheet accounts, carry forward. Many textbooks use an Income Summary account as a temporary holding place.
steps: Close revenue: debit Service Revenue 2,800; credit Income Summary 2,800.
Close expenses: debit Income Summary 1,230; credit each expense for its balance.
Close Income Summary: debit Income Summary 1,570; credit Owner's Capital 1,570. A net loss would reverse this entry.
Close drawing: debit Owner's Capital 300; credit Owner's Drawing 300. Drawing never goes through Income Summary.

example.scenario: Which accounts appear on Lantern's post-closing trial balance, and what are the totals?
example.solution: Only permanent accounts appear. Debits: Cash 3,600, A/R 650, Supplies 120, Prepaid Insurance 1,100, Equipment 2,400, totaling 7,870. Credits: Accumulated Depreciation 50, A/P 1,100, Wages Payable 200, Unearned Revenue 250, Capital 6,270, totaling 7,870. Total assets on the balance sheet are lower, at 7,820, because the balance sheet subtracts accumulated depreciation while the trial balance lists it as a credit.

sections.heading: Find and correct errors
paragraphs: A trial balance catches errors that make debits and credits unequal. It does not catch an omitted transaction, an entry recorded twice, an entry posted to the wrong account on the correct side, or two errors that cancel. Use the size of the difference as a clue.

To correct an error after posting, write a correcting entry. Do not erase. If a $450 utility bill was recorded as Rent Expense, debit Utilities Expense 450 and credit Rent Expense 450. Cash was correct, so it is not touched.
bullets: Difference divisible by 9: look for a transposition such as 96 recorded as 69 (difference 27) or a slide such as 450 recorded as 45.
Difference equal to twice an amount: an amount was posted to the wrong side. A $60 debit posted as a credit creates a $120 difference.
Difference equal to one amount: one side of an entry was not posted.

practice.task: Birch Tutoring's unadjusted balances include Service Revenue 3,000, Rent Expense 800, Supplies 400, and Prepaid Insurance 600 for a 6-month policy bought this month. Beginning capital is 2,000 and drawing is 500. At month end, $150 of supplies remain and employees earned $120 of unpaid wages. Record the adjustments, then find net income and ending capital.
practice.answer: Supplies Expense 250 / Supplies 250 (400 - 150). Insurance Expense 100 / Prepaid Insurance 100 (600 / 6). Wages Expense 120 / Wages Payable 120. Total expenses are 800 + 250 + 100 + 120 = 1,270. Net income is 3,000 - 1,270 = 1,730. Ending capital is 2,000 + 1,730 - 500 = 3,230.

terms.definition: A list of all account balances after adjusting entries, used to prepare the financial statements.
An account with a credit balance that reduces a related asset, such as Accumulated Depreciation.
A temporary account used during closing to collect revenues and expenses before the net amount moves to capital.
A trial balance prepared after closing that lists only permanent accounts.
A new journal entry that fixes an error already posted, leaving the original record visible.

questions.prompt: A customer pays $400 in May for work to be done in June. The May entry credits:
questions.explanation: The business owes future work, so the advance is a liability until earned.

questions.prompt: Which step comes immediately after preparing the financial statements?
questions.explanation: Statements use the revenue and expense balances, so closing happens after them.

questions.prompt: A trial balance is out of balance by $54. Which error is the most likely cause?
choices: A correct amount was posted to the wrong account on the correct side
$76 was recorded as $22 on one side only
questions.explanation: A one-sided error equal to the difference unbalances the totals. The other three errors leave the trial balance in balance.

questions.prompt: Equipment cost $3,600, has a 3-year life, and no salvage value. Monthly straight-line depreciation is:
questions.explanation: 3,600 / 3 = 1,200 per year, and 1,200 / 12 = 100 per month.

questions.prompt: Which account appears on a post-closing trial balance?
questions.explanation: Wages Payable is a liability, which is a permanent account. The others are closed to zero.

title: Purchasing, sales, and receivables
summary: Purchase documents, the three-way match, discounts, returns and allowances, and the methods for uncollectible accounts.

sections.heading: Follow the purchasing documents
paragraphs: A purchase passes through several documents so that no single person can order, receive, and pay for goods alone. Each document answers a different question. Tests often describe a document and ask for its name, or ask which document is compared with which.

Before paying, the accounts payable clerk performs a three-way match. The purchase order shows what was ordered and at what price. The receiving report shows what actually arrived. The vendor invoice shows what the vendor is billing. If all three agree, a voucher is approved for payment. In a voucher system, the approved voucher becomes the record that authorizes the check or electronic payment.

rows: Internal request asking purchasing to buy
Authorizes the vendor to ship at stated terms
Records quantity and condition of goods received
Approves payment after documents are matched
Notifies the vendor that the buyer is reducing the amount owed for a return or allowance
Notifies the customer that the seller is reducing the amount owed

sections.heading: Record purchases with terms and returns
paragraphs: Credit terms of 2/10, n/30 mean the buyer may take a 2% discount if it pays within 10 days. Otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days. The discount applies only to the amount still owed after returns. FOB shipping point means the buyer owns goods once they leave the seller and pays freight. FOB destination means the seller owns them until they arrive.
The entries below use a perpetual inventory system, where the Inventory account is updated with each purchase and sale.

example.scenario: Maple Hardware buys $2,000 of merchandise on account, terms 2/10, n/30. It returns $200 of damaged goods and pays the balance within the discount period.
steps: Purchase: debit Inventory 2,000; credit Accounts Payable 2,000.
Return: debit Accounts Payable 200; credit Inventory 200.
Balance owed: 2,000 - 200 = 1,800. Discount: 1,800 x 2% = 36.
Payment: debit Accounts Payable 1,800; credit Inventory 36; credit Cash 1,764.
example.solution: Maple pays $1,764. The discount lowers the cost of the inventory. Under a periodic system, the same amounts go to Purchases, Purchase Returns and Allowances, and Purchase Discounts instead of Inventory.

sections.heading: Record sales, returns, allowances, and discounts
paragraphs: A sale on account under a perpetual system needs two entries: one for the selling price and one for the cost of the goods. A sales return means goods come back. A sales allowance is a price reduction the customer accepts while keeping the goods. Sales Returns and Allowances and Sales Discounts are contra-revenue accounts with debit balances. Net sales equal gross sales minus both.

example.scenario: Maple sells goods for $1,500 on account, terms 2/10, n/30. The goods cost $900. The customer returns goods priced at $100 that cost $60, then receives a $50 allowance for a scratch, then pays within 10 days.
steps: Sale: debit Accounts Receivable 1,500; credit Sales 1,500. Debit Cost of Goods Sold 900; credit Inventory 900.
Return: debit Sales Returns and Allowances 100; credit Accounts Receivable 100. Debit Inventory 60; credit Cost of Goods Sold 60.
Allowance: debit Sales Returns and Allowances 50; credit Accounts Receivable 50. No inventory entry, because nothing came back.
Balance: 1,500 - 100 - 50 = 1,350. Discount: 1,350 x 2% = 27. Debit Cash 1,323; debit Sales Discounts 27; credit Accounts Receivable 1,350.
example.solution: Net sales are 1,500 - 150 - 27 = 1,323. Cost of goods sold is 900 - 60 = 840, so gross profit is 483.

sections.heading: Estimate and write off uncollectible accounts
paragraphs: Some customers will never pay. The direct write-off method records bad debt expense only when a specific account is judged uncollectible. It is simple and is used for tax purposes, but it is not allowed under GAAP when bad debts are material because the expense lands in a later period than the sale.

The allowance method estimates bad debts in the same period as the sales. The estimate is credited to Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, a contra-asset. Net realizable value is Accounts Receivable minus the allowance. When a specific account is later written off, debit the Allowance and credit Accounts Receivable. That write-off entry does not change expense or net realizable value.

The percentage-of-sales method multiplies credit sales by a rate and records that amount as expense, ignoring the existing allowance balance. The aging method estimates the required ending balance of the allowance, then records whatever adjustment reaches that balance.
bullets: If the allowance already has a $350 credit balance, the adjustment is 1,200 - 350 = $850.
If the allowance has a $100 debit balance because write-offs exceeded the estimate, the adjustment is 1,200 + 100 = $1,300.
If a written-off customer later pays, first reinstate the account (debit A/R, credit Allowance), then record the collection (debit Cash, credit A/R).

practice.task: A company has credit sales of $80,000 and receivables of $30,000. The allowance has a $350 credit balance. (a) Using 1% of credit sales, what is bad debt expense? (b) Using the aging table above, what is bad debt expense? (c) What is net realizable value after the aging adjustment?
practice.answer: (a) 80,000 x 1% = $800, regardless of the existing balance. (b) The required balance is $1,200, so the expense is 1,200 - 350 = $850. (c) Net realizable value is 30,000 - 1,200 = $28,800.

sections.heading: Control accounts and collection measures
paragraphs: The Accounts Receivable account in the general ledger is a control account. A subsidiary ledger keeps a separate account for each customer. At month end, the schedule of accounts receivable, which lists each customer's balance, must equal the control account. Accounts payable works the same way with a vendor subsidiary ledger.

Receivables turnover equals net credit sales divided by average accounts receivable. Days sales outstanding equals 365 divided by turnover. If net credit sales are $400,000 and average receivables are $40,000, turnover is 10 and customers take about 36.5 days to pay. If terms are n/30, the business should review its credit and collection policies.

terms.definition: Comparing the purchase order, receiving report, and vendor invoice before approving payment.
An internal document that authorizes payment after supporting documents are verified.
A price reduction given to a customer who keeps the goods.
A contra-asset holding the estimate of receivables that will not be collected.
Accounts receivable minus the allowance for doubtful accounts.
A table that groups receivables by how long they have been outstanding to estimate uncollectible amounts.

questions.prompt: Which document is prepared by the receiving department?
questions.explanation: The receiving report records what arrived and its condition.

questions.prompt: An invoice for $3,000 has terms 2/10, n/30. The buyer returns $500 of goods and pays within 10 days. The payment is:
questions.explanation: The discount applies to the $2,500 still owed: 2,500 x 0.98 = 2,450.

questions.prompt: Under the allowance method, writing off a specific $400 customer account:
questions.explanation: Both A/R and the allowance fall by $400, so their difference stays the same.

questions.prompt: An aging schedule requires a $2,000 allowance. The allowance has a $300 debit balance before adjustment. Bad debt expense is:
questions.explanation: The adjustment must cover the debit balance and reach a $2,000 credit balance: 2,000 + 300.

questions.prompt: Sales Returns and Allowances is best described as:
questions.explanation: It reduces gross sales to net sales and normally has a debit balance.

title: Payroll workbook: from timecard to tax deposit
summary: Calculate gross pay, deductions, net pay, and employer taxes, then journalize and remit them using dated practice assumptions.

sections.heading: Practice assumptions and where to check them
paragraphs: Payroll rates and limits change, so every number below is a stated practice assumption for 2026. Check IRS Publication 15 and the Social Security Administration before using any rate outside this lesson. On a test, use the rates the question gives you.

Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% of wages up to the yearly wage base, which the SSA set at $184,500 for 2026. Medicare tax is 1.45% of all wages with no limit, plus an additional 0.9% withheld from an employee's wages above $200,000 in a year. The employer matches Social Security and the regular 1.45% Medicare. Together these are called FICA. The federal unemployment tax (FUTA) is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, reduced to a net 0.6% when the employer receives the full state credit. State unemployment tax (SUTA) rates vary by state and employer. This lesson assumes 2.6%.

Federal and state income tax withholding come from the employee's Form W-4 and the IRS or state tables. Tests usually give you the withholding amount. Do not try to compute it unless the question supplies the table.

sections.heading: Calculate gross pay and taxable wages
paragraphs: The Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime of at least 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek for nonexempt employees. Exempt employees, usually salaried professionals and managers who meet duty and salary tests, are not owed overtime.

Deductions affect taxable wages differently. A traditional 401(k) contribution reduces wages subject to federal income tax withholding, but it is still subject to Social Security, Medicare, and FUTA. A Section 125 cafeteria plan health premium reduces wages for income tax, FICA, and FUTA. This difference is a common test question.

example.scenario: Rosa earns $18 an hour and works 46 hours in a week. She contributes 5% of gross pay to a traditional 401(k) and pays $30 for health insurance through a Section 125 plan. Her W-4 and the tables give federal withholding of $61.00 and state withholding of $30.00. Her year-to-date wages are well below every wage base.
steps: Regular pay: 40 x $18 = $720.00. Overtime rate: $18 x 1.5 = $27. Overtime pay: 6 x $27 = $162.00. Gross pay: $882.00.
FICA wages: 882 - 30 = $852.00. The 401(k) is not subtracted.
Social Security: 852 x 6.2% = $52.82. Medicare: 852 x 1.45% = $12.35.
example.solution: Rosa's check is $651.73. Her earnings record shows gross pay $882.00, each deduction, and net pay, and her year-to-date totals are updated.

sections.heading: Calculate employer payroll taxes
paragraphs: Employer taxes are an expense of the business and are never deducted from the employee. Using Rosa's $852 of FICA and FUTA wages, the employer owes Social Security 52.82, Medicare 12.35, FUTA 852 x 0.6% = 5.11, and SUTA 852 x 2.6% = 22.15. Total payroll tax expense is $92.43.

Wage bases matter near the limit. If an employee has already earned $183,000 in 2026 and earns $3,000 more, only 184,500 - 183,000 = $1,500 is subject to Social Security tax. All $3,000 is still subject to Medicare. FUTA stops for each employee once that employee's wages for the year pass $7,000.

sections.heading: Journalize the payroll and the deposits
paragraphs: The payroll entry records gross wages as expense and creates a liability for each amount withheld. The employer tax entry is separate. Later entries pay the employee and remit the withheld and employer taxes.

rows: Social Security Tax Payable 52.82; Medicare Tax Payable 12.35; Federal Income Tax Payable 61.00; State Income Tax Payable 30.00; 401(k) Payable 44.10; Health Insurance Payable 30.00; Wages Payable 651.73
Social Security Tax Payable 52.82; Medicare Tax Payable 12.35; FUTA Tax Payable 5.11; SUTA Tax Payable 22.15
Deposit federal taxes reported on Form 941
Federal Income Tax Payable 61.00; Social Security Tax Payable 105.64; Medicare Tax Payable 24.70

bullets: The federal deposit combines withheld income tax with both halves of FICA: 61.00 + (52.82 x 2) + (12.35 x 2) = 191.34.
FUTA is deposited separately and reported yearly on Form 940. SUTA goes to the state agency.
Check the totals: the credits in the payroll entry must add up to gross pay.

sections.heading: Payroll records and forms
paragraphs: The payroll register lists every employee for one pay period with hours, gross pay, each deduction, and net pay. The employee earnings record follows one employee across the whole year and supplies the year-to-date totals that tell you when a wage base is reached. Federal law requires employers to keep employment tax records for at least four years.

rows: Information used to figure federal income tax withholding
Identity and authorization to work (kept by employer, not sent to IRS)
Federal income tax withheld and FICA for the quarter
Employer to the Social Security Administration
Nonemployee compensation. Contractors are not on payroll and have no withholding.

practice.task: Dev earns $16 an hour and works 44 hours. There are no pre-tax deductions. Federal withholding is $38.00 and state withholding is $20.00. Using this lesson's assumptions, find gross pay, Social Security, Medicare, net pay, and the employer's total payroll tax expense.
practice.answer: Gross pay: 40 x 16 = 640, plus 4 x 24 = 96, for $736.00. Social Security: 736 x 6.2% = $45.63. Medicare: 736 x 1.45% = $10.67. Net pay: 736 - 45.63 - 10.67 - 38 - 20 = $621.70. Employer taxes: Social Security 45.63 + Medicare 10.67 + FUTA 4.42 (736 x 0.6%) + SUTA 19.14 (736 x 2.6%) = $79.86.

terms.definition: Federal Insurance Contributions Act taxes: Social Security and Medicare, paid by both employee and employer.
The maximum yearly wages subject to a particular tax, such as Social Security or FUTA.
An employee covered by FLSA overtime rules.
A summary of all employees' earnings and deductions for one pay period.
A cumulative record of one employee's pay and deductions for the year.

questions.prompt: A nonexempt worker earns $20 an hour and works 45 hours. Gross pay is:
A traditional 401(k) deferral reduces wages subject to:
questions.explanation: Elective 401(k) deferrals remain subject to FICA and FUTA.

questions.prompt: Which tax is paid only by the employer?
questions.explanation: FUTA is an employer tax and is never withheld from the employee.

questions.prompt: Which form reports quarterly federal income tax withholding and FICA?
questions.explanation: Form 941 is the Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return.

questions.prompt: In the payroll journal entry, the amounts withheld from employees are recorded as:
questions.explanation: Withholdings are owed to governments and other parties until they are paid.

title: Inventory costing, adjustments, and errors
summary: Compute FIFO, LIFO, and weighted-average results from one dataset, then handle returns, shrinkage, write-downs, and inventory errors.

sections.heading: One dataset, three answers
paragraphs: Cost flow methods decide which unit costs go to cost of goods sold and which stay in ending inventory. They do not have to match the physical flow of goods. The total cost of goods available for sale is always split between the two, so ending inventory plus cost of goods sold equals goods available under every method.

Use this periodic dataset for Trailhead Outfitters. Beginning inventory is 100 units at $10. Purchases are 200 units at $11 in March, 150 units at $12 in June, and 50 units at $13 in September. Goods available are 500 units costing 1,000 + 2,200 + 1,800 + 650 = $5,650. The store sold 380 units at $20 each, so 120 units remain.
bullets: When prices rise, FIFO gives the highest ending inventory and net income. LIFO gives the highest cost of goods sold and the lowest taxable income.
U.S. GAAP allows LIFO, but IFRS does not. A company that uses LIFO for taxes must also use it for financial reports, called the LIFO conformity rule.
Specific identification tracks the actual cost of each unit. It suits unique, high-value items such as cars or jewelry.

sections.heading: Periodic and perpetual systems
paragraphs: A periodic system updates inventory only after a physical count at the end of the period. Purchases go to a Purchases account, and cost of goods sold is calculated as beginning inventory plus net purchases minus ending inventory. A perpetual system updates Inventory and Cost of Goods Sold with every sale, usually through point-of-sale scanning.

FIFO gives the same answer under both systems. LIFO and average cost can differ because a perpetual system uses only the units on hand at the moment of each sale. If a question says perpetual LIFO, work through each sale in date order.

sections.heading: Returns, shrinkage, and write-downs
paragraphs: A purchase return reduces Inventory in a perpetual system. A customer return puts the goods back into Inventory at their cost and reduces Cost of Goods Sold, but only if the goods can be resold.

Shrinkage is the loss of inventory from theft, damage, or recording errors. It is found by comparing the perpetual record with a physical count. If records show inventory costing $1,560 and the count values it at $1,490, debit Cost of Goods Sold (or Inventory Shrinkage) $70 and credit Inventory $70. Shrinkage rate is the loss divided by the recorded amount: 70 / 1,560 = 4.5%.

Obsolete or damaged goods may be worth less than they cost. Under FIFO and average cost, inventory is reported at the lower of cost and net realizable value. Net realizable value is the expected selling price minus the costs to complete and sell. Companies using LIFO or the retail method use a lower of cost or market rule instead.

example.scenario: Trailhead holds 30 last-season jackets that cost $40 each. They can now sell for $45, but selling them will require $8 each in markdown advertising and shipping.
example.solution: Net realizable value is 45 - 8 = $37, which is below the $40 cost. Write down 30 x $3 = $90: debit Cost of Goods Sold (or Loss on Inventory Write-Down) 90; credit Inventory 90. The jackets are then carried at $37 each.

sections.heading: Inventory errors and turnover
paragraphs: Because ending inventory is subtracted to find cost of goods sold, an error in ending inventory moves net income in the same direction. If ending inventory is overstated by $500, cost of goods sold is understated by $500 and net income is overstated by $500. That ending inventory becomes next year's beginning inventory, so next year's income is understated by $500. Over the two years the error cancels, but both years' statements are wrong.

Inventory turnover equals cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. Days in inventory equals 365 divided by turnover. A grocery store has high turnover; a furniture store has low turnover. Compare a company with its own history and its industry rather than with unrelated businesses.

practice.task: Beginning inventory is 40 units at $5. The company buys 60 units at $6, then 50 units at $7. It sells 90 units using a periodic system. Find ending inventory and cost of goods sold under FIFO, LIFO, and weighted average.
practice.answer: Goods available: 150 units costing 200 + 360 + 350 = $910. Ending inventory is 60 units. FIFO: 50 x 7 + 10 x 6 = $410 ending; COGS $500. LIFO: 40 x 5 + 20 x 6 = $320 ending; COGS $590. Weighted average: 910 / 150 = $6.0667 per unit; ending 60 x 6.0667 = $364; COGS 90 x 6.0667 = $546. Each pair adds to $910.

terms.definition: First-in, first-out: the oldest costs are assigned to cost of goods sold first.
Last-in, first-out: the newest costs are assigned to cost of goods sold first.
Beginning inventory plus net purchases for the period.
Inventory loss from theft, damage, or errors, found by comparing records with a count.
Estimated selling price minus the costs needed to complete and sell the item.

questions.prompt: During a period of rising prices, which method reports the lowest cost of goods sold?
choices: All methods give the same result
questions.explanation: FIFO sends the older, cheaper costs to cost of goods sold.

questions.prompt: Goods available cost $8,000 and ending inventory is $1,900. Cost of goods sold is:
questions.explanation: COGS equals goods available minus ending inventory.

questions.prompt: Ending inventory is understated by $300. This year's net income is:
questions.explanation: Lower ending inventory raises COGS, which lowers net income by the same amount.

questions.prompt: Which accounting framework prohibits LIFO?
questions.explanation: International Financial Reporting Standards do not allow LIFO.

questions.prompt: An item costs $60, sells for $70, and needs $15 of selling costs. Its carrying value under lower of cost and NRV is:
questions.explanation: NRV is 70 - 15 = 55, which is lower than cost.

title: Standards, tax records, software, and accounting careers
summary: GAAP and the bodies behind it, sales and income tax entries, accounting software controls, annual report disclosures, and professional paths.

sections.heading: Who sets the rules
paragraphs: Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) are the rules U.S. businesses follow for financial reports. The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) sets GAAP for businesses and nonprofits. The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) sets standards for state and local governments. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has legal authority over public company reporting and relies on FASB. The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) issues IFRS, which most other countries use.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 followed the Enron and WorldCom frauds. It created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to oversee auditors of public companies, requires executives to certify financial reports, and requires management to report on internal control over financial reporting.

rows: Business records are kept separate from the owner's
The owner's personal car payment is not a business expense
Assume the business will keep operating
Equipment is depreciated over its useful life instead of shown at liquidation value
Record only items measurable in money
Employee morale is not recorded as an asset
Divide the business's life into reporting periods
Record assets at their purchase cost
Land bought for $80,000 stays at $80,000 even if its value rises
Record revenue when the performance obligation is satisfied
A gym records a yearly fee one month at a time
Record expenses in the period of the revenue they helped earn
Sales commissions are recorded in the month of the sale
Report information that would change a user's decision
A pending lawsuit is described in the notes

bullets: The two fundamental qualities of useful information are relevance and faithful representation.
The enhancing qualities are comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability.

sections.heading: Tax accounting records
paragraphs: Sales tax collected from customers belongs to the state, so it is a liability. Maryland's general sales tax rate has been 6%; use the rate the question gives. A $500 taxable sale is recorded as debit Cash 530, credit Sales 500, credit Sales Tax Payable 30. Paying the state debits Sales Tax Payable and credits Cash. Sales tax is never revenue.

The form of business decides how income tax is filed. A sole proprietor reports business profit on Schedule C with the owner's Form 1040 and pays self-employment tax. A partnership files Form 1065 and gives each partner a Schedule K-1; the partners pay the tax. A C corporation files Form 1120 and pays a flat 21% federal rate under current law. An S corporation files Form 1120-S and passes income to shareholders. Owners without withholding generally make quarterly estimated payments.

Tax rules and financial accounting rules can differ. A company may use straight-line depreciation for its statements and the faster MACRS method on its tax return. Differences that reverse over time create deferred tax amounts. The IRS generally recommends keeping records supporting a return for three years after filing, longer in some situations, and employment tax records for at least four years.

example.scenario: A client who runs a small bakery wants to deduct the family's grocery bill and has lost several supplier receipts.
example.solution: Explain that personal expenses are not business deductions under the economic entity concept and tax law. Help the client rebuild records from bank and card statements and supplier copies, and set up a system that separates business and personal accounts. Do not invent amounts or dates.

sections.heading: Accounting software and its controls
paragraphs: Accounting software records the same debits and credits as a paper journal, but it posts automatically and produces reports instantly. Setting it up correctly matters more than learning menus. Build the chart of accounts first, enter opening balances, connect bank feeds if available, and set user permissions so that the person who records bills is not the person who approves payments.

An audit trail, sometimes called audit history, records who created, changed, or deleted each transaction and when. A good practice is to correct a posted transaction with a reversing or adjusting entry instead of editing it, especially after a period is closed. Most programs let an administrator set a closing date and require a password to change anything before it.
steps: Enter a sample invoice, a bill, and a payment in a practice company file.
Run the trial balance, income statement, and accounts receivable aging report, and check that totals match your manual calculation.
Correct one deliberate error with an adjusting entry, then open the audit trail and find both the original and the correction.
Back up the company file, change a record, restore the backup, and confirm the change is gone. A backup that has never been restored has not been tested.
Set a closing date and confirm that a new entry dated in the closed period is blocked or requires approval.

sections.heading: Annual reports and disclosure
paragraphs: A public company's annual report to the SEC is Form 10-K. It includes a business description, risk factors, management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), audited financial statements, notes, and the auditor's report. The notes explain accounting policies, such as the inventory method, and give details that the statements cannot show, such as debt terms and lawsuits.

The auditor's opinion tells readers how much to trust the statements. An unmodified (clean) opinion says the statements are fairly presented. A qualified opinion says they are fair except for a specific matter. An adverse opinion says they are not fairly presented. A disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion.

sections.heading: Careers and professional organizations
paragraphs: Accounting careers include public accounting (audit, tax, and advisory work for clients), corporate or managerial accounting, government accounting, and forensic accounting. The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook gives current duties, pay, and job outlook.

rows: State boards of accountancy (exam by AICPA and NASBA)
Licensed to sign audit opinions; requirements are set by each state and have changed in recent years

practice.task: Classify each item: (a) A company records a $900 sales tax collection as revenue. (b) A business lists land at its current appraised value. (c) A shop records a 12-month service contract as revenue on the day it is paid. Name the rule each one breaks and the correct treatment.
practice.answer: (a) Sales tax is a liability owed to the state: credit Sales Tax Payable, not Sales. (b) The historical cost principle keeps land at its purchase cost. (c) Revenue recognition: record the cash as Unearned Revenue and recognize one-twelfth each month as the service is provided.

terms.definition: Generally accepted accounting principles, the U.S. rules for financial reporting.
Financial Accounting Standards Board, the private body that sets U.S. GAAP for businesses and nonprofits.
A record showing who entered or changed each transaction and when.
The annual report a public company files with the SEC.
An auditor's conclusion that the financial statements are fairly presented.

questions.prompt: Which body sets accounting standards for state and local governments?
questions.explanation: The Governmental Accounting Standards Board covers state and local governments.

questions.prompt: A $200 taxable sale with 6% sales tax is collected in cash. The credit to Sales Tax Payable is:
questions.explanation: 200 x 6% = 12, which is owed to the state.

questions.prompt: Which law created the PCAOB?
questions.explanation: Sarbanes-Oxley (2002) created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board.

questions.prompt: The best way to test a software backup is to:
choices: Restore it and confirm the data
Back it up a second time
questions.explanation: Only a successful restore proves the backup can be used.

questions.prompt: Recording an owner's personal expenses as business expenses violates the:
questions.explanation: The economic entity assumption keeps business and personal records separate.

title: Cash flow statements and financial ratios
summary: Build a statement of cash flows with the indirect method, then calculate and interpret profitability, liquidity, efficiency, and solvency ratios.

sections.heading: The three sections of the cash flow statement
paragraphs: Net income and cash are different because accrual accounting records revenue and expenses when earned and incurred. The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash in three sections. Operating activities come from the main business. Investing activities buy and sell long-term assets and investments. Financing activities raise or repay money from owners and lenders.

Under U.S. GAAP, interest paid and interest and dividends received are operating cash flows, while dividends paid are financing. The indirect method starts with net income and adjusts it to cash. It is the method most companies use.

rows: Repaying loan principal or paying dividends

sections.heading: Work the indirect method
paragraphs: Add back expenses that used no cash, such as depreciation. Subtract gains on asset sales because the full sale proceeds belong in investing. For current operating assets, an increase means cash was tied up, so subtract it. For current operating liabilities, an increase means the company kept cash, so add it.

example.scenario: Northgate Supply reports net income of $50,000 and depreciation of $12,000. It sold equipment for $10,000 cash at a $4,000 gain. Accounts receivable rose $8,000, inventory fell $5,000, accounts payable rose $3,000, and accrued liabilities fell $2,000. It bought new equipment for $30,000, issued stock for $15,000, repaid $12,000 of a loan, and paid $9,000 in dividends. Beginning cash was $18,000.
example.solution: Ending cash is $48,000. Free cash flow, a common measure of cash available after keeping the business running, is operating cash flow minus capital expenditures: 56,000 - 30,000 = $26,000.

sections.heading: Calculate the core ratios
paragraphs: Use this fictional data for every ratio below. Revenue is $400,000, cost of goods sold $240,000, operating income $60,000, interest expense $6,000, and net income $40,000. Current assets are $120,000 (cash $30,000, receivables $40,000, inventory $50,000). Current liabilities are $80,000. Total liabilities are $200,000 and equity is $300,000. Averages for the year are inventory $48,000, receivables $38,000, total assets $480,000, and equity $290,000.

rows: Share of each sales dollar left after product cost
Profit from operations before interest and taxes
Profit kept from each sales dollar
Profit earned on the owners' investment
Sales produced per dollar of assets
How much the company relies on borrowing

bullets: The DuPont model splits return on equity: net margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier. Here 0.10 x 0.833 x (480,000 / 290,000 = 1.655) = 13.8%.

Horizontal analysis compares a line across years: revenue rising from $360,000 to $400,000 is an 11.1% increase. Vertical analysis states each line as a percent of a base, such as cost of goods sold equal to 60% of revenue.

sections.heading: Interpret instead of only calculating
paragraphs: A ratio means little alone. Compare it with the company's prior years, with close competitors, and with industry figures. A current ratio of 1.5 may be comfortable for a manufacturer and unnecessary for a grocery chain that collects cash daily. A falling inventory turnover could mean weaker demand or a deliberate build-up before a busy season. Read the notes and MD&A to learn which explanation is true.
State conclusions with evidence: name the ratio, the change, the likely cause, and what you would check next. Avoid saying a company is healthy or weak based on one number.

practice.task: A company has current assets of $90,000 including $25,000 of inventory, current liabilities of $60,000, net income of $18,000, revenue of $240,000, and average equity of $150,000. Calculate the current ratio, quick ratio (assume all other current assets are cash and receivables), net margin, and return on equity. Then write one sentence interpreting the quick ratio.
practice.answer: Current ratio: 90,000 / 60,000 = 1.50. Quick ratio: (90,000 - 25,000) / 60,000 = 1.08. Net margin: 18,000 / 240,000 = 7.5%. ROE: 18,000 / 150,000 = 12%. Interpretation: the company could pay its current liabilities from cash and receivables alone, without relying on selling inventory, though the result should be compared with prior years and the industry.

terms.definition: A way of reporting operating cash flow that starts with net income and adjusts for noncash items and working capital changes.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.
Cash, short-term investments, and receivables divided by current liabilities.
Net income divided by average shareholders' equity.
Comparing financial statement amounts across periods, usually as percent changes.

questions.prompt: Under U.S. GAAP, dividends paid are reported in:
questions.explanation: Payments to owners are financing activities.

questions.prompt: In the indirect method, an increase in accounts receivable is:
questions.explanation: Revenue was recorded but cash was not collected, so cash is lower than net income.

questions.prompt: Operating cash flow is $80,000 and capital expenditures are $35,000. Free cash flow is:
Cost of goods sold is $300,000 and average inventory is $60,000. Inventory turnover is:
Which ratio best measures a company's reliance on borrowed money?
questions.explanation: Debt-to-equity compares total liabilities with owners' equity.

title: Managerial accounting: cost behavior, decisions, variances, and controls
summary: Break-even and target profit, relevant costs for special orders and make-or-buy, standard cost variances, overhead rates, and internal control cases.

sections.heading: Cost-volume-profit analysis
paragraphs: Managerial accounting produces information for decisions inside the business. It starts with cost behavior. Variable costs change in total with volume, such as materials. Fixed costs stay the same in total within a relevant range, such as rent. Contribution margin is price minus variable cost per unit. It is the amount each unit contributes toward fixed costs and then profit.

example.scenario: A fictional water-bottle maker sells bottles for $50. Variable cost is $30 per bottle and fixed costs are $60,000 a year. Expected sales are 3,600 bottles.
steps: Contribution margin per unit: 50 - 30 = $20. Contribution margin ratio: 20 / 50 = 40%.
Break-even units: 60,000 / 20 = 3,000 bottles. Break-even sales: 60,000 / 0.40 = $150,000.
Units for a $20,000 target profit: (60,000 + 20,000) / 20 = 4,000 bottles.
Margin of safety: (3,600 - 3,000) / 3,600 = 16.7% of expected sales.
example.solution: The company breaks even at 3,000 bottles and has a 16.7% cushion at expected volume. If fixed costs rose, break-even would rise; if price rose, contribution margin and profit per unit would rise.

sections.heading: Use relevant costs for decisions
paragraphs: A relevant cost differs between the alternatives and occurs in the future. Sunk costs, which were already spent, are never relevant. Fixed costs that continue no matter what is chosen are also not relevant. Opportunity cost, which is the benefit lost by not choosing the next best option, is relevant even though it never appears in the accounting records.
Marginal analysis applies the same idea one unit at a time. Keep producing as long as the revenue from one more unit is greater than the cost of that unit.

rows: Idle capacity; customer offers $38 for 500 units; variable cost $30 plus $2 special shipping
Accept: +$3,000, if regular prices are not affected
Make: $12 variable plus $2 of avoidable fixed cost per unit. Allocated fixed cost of $4 remains either way. Buy: $15
Make, unless the freed space could earn more than $1 per unit
Product line loses $5,000 after $12,000 of allocated fixed costs that would remain
Lost contribution margin of $7,000 versus no savings
Keep the line; dropping it lowers total profit by $7,000

sections.heading: Apply overhead and calculate variances
paragraphs: A predetermined overhead rate assigns indirect costs to products. If estimated overhead is $240,000 and the company expects 12,000 direct labor hours, the rate is $20 per hour. A job using 30 hours is charged $600 of overhead. At year end, the difference between actual and applied overhead is underapplied (actual higher) or overapplied (actual lower). Job order costing tracks costs by individual job; process costing averages costs across identical units.

A standard cost is what a unit should cost. A variance is the difference between actual and standard. A favorable variance (F) means actual cost was lower; unfavorable (U) means it was higher. Always find the standard quantity allowed for the actual output first.

example.scenario: Each unit should use 2 pounds of material at $4 a pound and 0.5 labor hours at $20 an hour. The company made 1,000 units, using 2,100 pounds bought at $3.90 and 520 labor hours paid at $21.
steps: Standard quantities allowed: 1,000 x 2 = 2,000 pounds; 1,000 x 0.5 = 500 hours.
Material price variance: (3.90 - 4.00) x 2,100 = $210 F.
Material quantity variance: (2,100 - 2,000) x 4.00 = $400 U. Total material variance: $190 U (actual 8,190 versus standard 8,000).
Labor rate variance: (21 - 20) x 520 = $520 U.
Labor efficiency variance: (520 - 500) x 20 = $400 U. Total labor variance: $920 U (actual 10,920 versus standard 10,000).
example.solution: Cheaper material may have been lower quality, which could explain the extra pounds used. Investigate variances as connected clues rather than blaming one department automatically.

sections.heading: Internal controls and audit cases
paragraphs: Internal controls protect assets and make records reliable. The fraud triangle explains why fraud happens: pressure, opportunity, and rationalization. Controls mainly reduce opportunity.
Use the control principles to fix each case: establish responsibility, separate duties, document transactions, protect physical assets, verify independently, and rotate duties or require vacations.

rows: One clerk receives customer checks, records payments, and reconciles the bank account
Lapping: a clerk can steal one customer's payment and cover it with the next
Separate cash handling from recording and reconciliation
Payroll includes a worker no supervisor recognizes
HR adds employees; payroll pays them; supervisors approve hours
The petty cash box has no receipts for $140 of spending
Require receipts and an imprest fund replenished only for documented spending
The same employee has never taken a vacation in six years
Concealed errors or fraud may continue

practice.task: A product should use 3 hours of labor at $18 an hour. The company made 400 units using 1,150 hours paid at $18.50. Calculate the labor rate and efficiency variances and say whether each is favorable or unfavorable.
practice.answer: Standard hours allowed: 400 x 3 = 1,200. Rate variance: (18.50 - 18.00) x 1,150 = $575 U. Efficiency variance: (1,150 - 1,200) x 18 = $900 F. Total: $325 F. Actual cost 21,275 versus standard 21,600 confirms the total.

terms.definition: Selling price minus variable cost per unit, available to cover fixed costs and profit.
The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero.
A future cost that differs between alternatives.
A cost already incurred that cannot be changed by any decision.
The expected cost of producing one unit under normal conditions.
Assigning authorization, custody, and recordkeeping to different people.

questions.prompt: Price is $40, variable cost is $25, and fixed costs are $45,000. Break-even units are:
Which cost is irrelevant to a make-or-buy decision?
choices: Direct materials to make the part
Fixed costs that continue under both choices
Rent the freed space could earn
questions.explanation: Costs that do not differ between alternatives do not affect the choice.

questions.prompt: Actual price $5.20, standard price $5.00, actual quantity 1,000 pounds. The material price variance is:
questions.explanation: (5.20 - 5.00) x 1,000 = 200, and paying more than standard is unfavorable.

questions.prompt: Which element of the fraud triangle do internal controls mainly reduce?
questions.explanation: Controls make it harder to commit and hide fraud.

questions.prompt: Estimated overhead is $180,000 and estimated machine hours are 9,000. A job uses 25 machine hours. Applied overhead is:
questions.explanation: The rate is 180,000 / 9,000 = $20 per hour, and 25 x 20 = 500.

title: Banking institutions, history, and regulation
summary: Compare financial institutions and markets, trace the laws that shaped U.S. banking, and match each regulator and rule to what it controls.

sections.heading: Money and the financial system
paragraphs: Money has three functions. It is a medium of exchange, a unit of account for comparing values, and a store of value. Good money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply, and widely accepted. Banks are financial intermediaries: they take deposits from savers and lend to borrowers, earning the spread between the interest they charge and the interest they pay.

The money market trades short-term debt of one year or less, such as Treasury bills and commercial paper. The capital market trades long-term stocks and bonds. In the primary market, securities are sold for the first time and the money goes to the issuer. In the secondary market, investors trade with each other.

rows: NCUA, through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund
Consumer and business loans; no deposits

bullets: FDIC and NCUA insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured institution, for each ownership category.

Consolidation means fewer, larger institutions through mergers. Reasons include economies of scale, technology costs, and geographic reach. Concerns include less local lending and institutions that are too big to fail.

sections.heading: A timeline of U.S. banking
paragraphs: Tests often ask which law created an agency or ended a practice. Learn each law by the problem it answered.

rows: First Bank of the United States
A national bank promoted by Alexander Hamilton; its charter ended in 1811
Second Bank of the United States
Rechartered a national bank; President Andrew Jackson opposed it and its charter ended in 1836
National Currency and National Bank Acts
Created national bank charters, a national currency, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Created the Federal Reserve as the central bank after repeated banking panics
Created the FDIC and separated commercial banking from investment banking
Requires banks to help meet credit needs of their whole community, including low- and moderate-income areas
Repealed the Glass-Steagall separation and set financial privacy rules
Created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and the Financial Stability Oversight Council after the 2008 crisis

sections.heading: The regulators
paragraphs: The United States has a dual banking system. A bank can hold a national charter from the OCC or a state charter from a state banking department. In Maryland, the state regulator is the Office of Financial Regulation. Every bank also has a federal regulator.

The Federal Reserve has a Board of Governors in Washington with seven members serving 14-year terms, and 12 regional Reserve Banks. The Federal Open Market Committee sets monetary policy. The Fed's tools are open market operations (buying and selling government securities), the discount rate charged on loans to banks, and interest paid on reserve balances. Reserve requirements have been set at zero since March 2020.

rows: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Central bank; supervises state member banks and bank holding companies
Insures deposits; supervises state banks that are not Fed members; resolves failed banks
Charters federal credit unions and insures credit union shares
Writes and enforces consumer financial protection rules for large institutions and nonbank lenders
Treasury bureau that enforces anti-money-laundering rules

sections.heading: Lending, operations, and electronic rules
paragraphs: Compliance questions usually describe a situation and ask which rule applies. Group the rules by the activity they control.

rows: Lenders must disclose the APR and finance charge before credit is extended
No discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance
Accuracy, consumer access, and notice when a report leads to denial
Lenders report data used to detect discriminatory patterns
Disclose fees and the annual percentage yield (APY)
Sets the maximum time a bank may hold deposited funds; dollar amounts are adjusted for inflation
Error resolution and limits on consumer liability, which depend on how quickly a lost card is reported
Bank Secrecy Act and USA PATRIOT Act
Currency Transaction Report for cash over $10,000 in a day; Suspicious Activity Reports; customer identification
Electronic signatures and disclosures are valid when the consumer consents

bullets: Structuring, which means splitting cash deposits to avoid a Currency Transaction Report, is itself a federal crime. Tellers may not advise customers how to avoid a report.
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires privacy notices and safeguards for customer information.

practice.task: Name the rule or agency for each case. (a) A customer asks why a loan disclosure shows 7.2% when the advertised rate was 6.9%. (b) A customer deposits $9,500 cash on Monday and $9,500 on Tuesday and asks if that avoids paperwork. (c) A state-chartered bank that is not a Fed member is examined. (d) A customer disputes an unauthorized debit card charge.
practice.answer: (a) Truth in Lending (Regulation Z): the APR includes certain fees, so it can be higher than the note rate. (b) Bank Secrecy Act: deliberate splitting is structuring, which is illegal, and the activity may require a Suspicious Activity Report. (c) The FDIC supervises state nonmember banks, along with the state regulator. (d) Regulation E governs error resolution for electronic transfers.

example.scenario: A loan officer asks an applicant whether she plans to have children before approving a car loan.
example.solution: This violates the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, which bars decisions based on sex and marital status and limits questions about childbearing plans. The officer should evaluate income, debts, credit history, and collateral only.

terms.definition: An institution that moves funds from savers to borrowers.
The U.S. arrangement in which banks may be chartered by either the federal government or a state.
The Federal Reserve's buying and selling of government securities to influence interest rates.
A report banks file for cash transactions over $10,000 in one business day.
Annual percentage yield: the yearly return on a deposit including compounding.

questions.prompt: Which law created the FDIC?
questions.explanation: The Banking Act of 1933, often called Glass-Steagall, created federal deposit insurance.

questions.prompt: Which agency charters and supervises national banks?
questions.explanation: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency was created by the National Bank Acts.

questions.prompt: A credit union differs from a commercial bank mainly because it is:
questions.explanation: Credit unions are member-owned cooperatives insured through the NCUA.

questions.prompt: Which rule requires lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate?
questions.explanation: Regulation Z implements the Truth in Lending Act.

questions.prompt: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 created the:
questions.explanation: Dodd-Frank responded to the 2008 crisis and created the CFPB.

title: Teller operations, lending, and banking calculations
summary: Handle checks and cash, balance a drawer, spot fraud, analyze a loan application, and compute interest, APY, and loan payments.

sections.heading: Check and cash handling
paragraphs: A check's bottom line is the MICR line, printed in magnetic ink. It shows the 9-digit routing number that identifies the bank, the account number, and the check number. Before cashing a check, a teller verifies the customer's identity, confirms the written amount matches the numeric amount, checks the date and signature, and confirms that funds are available when the check is drawn on the teller's own bank.

Endorsements transfer a check. A blank endorsement is only a signature, so anyone holding the check can cash it. A restrictive endorsement such as "For deposit only" limits further use and is the safest choice for mailed deposits. A special endorsement names a new payee: "Pay to the order of Jordan Lee," then the signature. A check more than six months old is stale-dated, and a bank may refuse it. A postdated check carries a future date.
bullets: Counterfeit currency warning signs: missing security thread or watermark, color-shifting ink that does not shift, and flat, blurry printing.

Check fraud warning signs: altered amounts or payee names, a new account receiving large deposits followed by quick withdrawals, and overpayment requests where a stranger asks the customer to send back the difference.
Elder financial exploitation warning signs: an older customer making unusual withdrawals while accompanied by someone who answers for them. Follow the bank's escalation procedure.

sections.heading: Balance a teller drawer
paragraphs: At the start of a shift, the teller counts and signs for a starting amount. During the day, the teller records cash received and paid out. At the end, the expected balance is the beginning cash plus cash in minus cash out. The teller counts the drawer and compares. A difference is recorded as cash over or cash short and reported to a supervisor. A teller never covers a shortage with personal money.

example.scenario: A drawer starts with $2,500. During the shift the teller receives $3,180 in cash deposits and loan payments and pays out $2,940 in withdrawals and cashed checks. The ending count is $2,730.
example.solution: The drawer is $10 short. The teller recounts, reviews the day's transactions for a keying error, and reports the shortage under the bank's policy.

sections.heading: Analyze a loan application
paragraphs: Lenders judge credit using the five Cs. Character is the borrower's history of repaying, shown in the credit report and score. Capacity is the ability to repay from income, measured by the debt-to-income ratio. Capital is the borrower's own money in the deal, such as a down payment. Collateral is property the lender can claim if the loan is not repaid. Conditions are the loan's purpose and the economic environment.

Debt-to-income (DTI) equals monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income. Loan-to-value (LTV) equals the loan amount divided by the appraised value of the collateral. Lower DTI and LTV mean lower risk.

Loan structure includes the term, the payment schedule, whether the loan is secured, and whether the rate is fixed or variable. A variable rate is often set as an index such as the prime rate plus a margin. Risk-based pricing charges a higher rate to borrowers with weaker credit. Explain the terms to the client in plain language and give the required disclosures.

example.scenario: An applicant earns $6,000 a month before taxes. Monthly debts would be a $1,500 mortgage, a $400 car payment, and a $300 student loan. A home appraises at $250,000 and the requested mortgage is $225,000.
